DEPARTMENT OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION B-National Gallery of Canada-
548.	Payment to the national gallery purchase account for the purpose of acquiring works of art in conformity with section 8 of the National Gallery Act-further amount required, $885,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Shall this resolution carry?

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, further to some remarks I made on this item yesterday regarding the purchase of these paintings from the Prince of Liechtenstein, there are one or two further questions I should like to place before the minister, and I hope to get some answers. This is a very extensive item indeed for the purchase of paintings. We have heard that in the past deception has been going on in the purchase of paintings. For instance, it is a well known story that the late lamented Hermann Goering was properly swindled in the purchase of paintings once by a very great expert reproducer of old masters. I am not suggesting that the paintings of the Prince of Liechtenstein are in that class, but I would like to know how many experts, if any, examined this collection to make sure that they are what they are supposed to be. That is something that is well worth looking into. Did Mr. Jarvis, the director of the national gallery, see these pictures, or did the agent of the broker through whom they were bought examine them? Just who did examine these pictures? That is information the committee is entitled to. In addition to that, would the minister give us the name of the firm of brokers through whom those pictures were purchased?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the brokers were Agnew and Sons Limited, London, England.
As to the former question, my recollection is that the prince's collection of paintings is probably as well authenticated as almost any, in that there have been records of the paintings published over several hundred years, and that in questioning the background there is less chance of that occurring under these circumstances than would be if there were no record kept for some considerable time.
As to the number of experts who examined these paintings, I must say that I have not the information; but I do know that long before the current series of purchases began three or four years ago, the prince's collection had been examined not only by experts on behalf of the national gallery but by the

director of the national gallery himself on more than one occasion and at a time when probably it was not in their minds that we would be purchasing some of the paintings. However, on the main estimates I think the minister will give my hon. friend full details as to the steps taken to ensure that there is no mistake made.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I should like to follow up that question. Is it the purpose of the trustees of the national gallery to endeavour to the utmost to encourage the development and expansion of Canadian art? I ask this question because when I look at the expenditures that have been made since 1945 it is apparent that for every $22 spent on pictures painted elsewhere than in Canada, $1 is spent on Canadian paintings. I feel that a larger percentage of the expenditures should be directed to the encouragement of Canadian art. Canadian artists have a very difficult time to make their way. While they are impelled by their art, none the less they have to make a livelihood. When they have paintings that are worthy of the national gallery as being representative of Canada, indeed representative of Canadian nationalism, I feel that more encouragement should be given to them than has been given heretofore. If we are to build here in Ottawa a great national shrine, one that will memorialize our achievements, I feel that to a greater extent than ever before there must be as a target on the part of those charged with transforming Ottawa into the city beautiful, the national capital, a greater emphasis on things Canadian.
We have many French Canadian artists whose work is directed to the perpetuation of the life of the areas occupied in the main by those of French origin.
We have an important artist who comes from the province of Saskatchewan whose name is Henderson, a man who was laughed at when he first started to paint the barrenness of Saskatchewan. That was the view of those with a classically artistic turn of mind. He was able to perpetuate in art something of the spirit of Saskatchewan which to those who live in other provinces is difficult to discern on a visit there. He caught this spirit very imaginatively. It is the same with artists in other parts of this country. Another example is Miss Emily Carr whose art made her famous in her lifetime. I believe her work will live as representative of the generation in which she participated in the artistic life of this country.
With all due regard to the benefits that flow from viewing art for art's sake and pictures that are painted outside of our country, I feel that first and foremost the
Supply-National Gallery national gallery in the capital city should be one to encourage, develop and expand Canadian art.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I must say that I cannot get too enthusiastic about this expenditure, despite the fact that I may be accused of lacking culture. Nevertheless when I look at the sum of $885,000 for four paintings I begin to wonder if the government is bringing Liechtenstein into the Colombo plan, or if we are extending them lend-lease or something of that nature. In the original estimates the government proposed to spend $130,000 for acquiring art works this year. Parliament passed the policy on the basis of such a figure, and it seems rather strange to me that the government now comes and asks, in addition, seven times as much as the original sum.
The national gallery has a new director. I understand that Mr. Jarvis is an extremely capable man. Sometimes he likes to make speeches. Down in Montreal a few weeks ago he was apparently rather disdainful about hardware merchants and others who take it upon themselves to criticize expenditures for art. There may be some justification for his disdain and certainly he is entitled to his opinion. But I would remind Mr. Jarvis that it is the people of the constituency I represent and others, who have to pay the bills for these paintings. Indeed it is these people who pay his salary. I therefore think we are perfectly entitled to be critical at times of his spending.
What does the expenditure of $885,000 mean in terms of farming? I would point out that it represents about 650,000 bushels of wheat, the total output of approximately 125 prairie farmers for a year. It represents about 6,000 steers, I suppose-grain-fed ones at that. I think this sum is a lot of money and I wonder if it is wisely spent.
I have been told that we have literally thousands of paintings at the gallery today which are not on display. Some are stored in the basement and some are stored in other warehouses. I do not know whether or not this is correct, but if it is, I feel we should take some action to put on display the paintings which are presently in storage, before we expend such huge sums in purchasing additional works.
I should like to ask the minister what is being done to get these art treasures out to other parts of the country, so people other than those living in Ottawa can see them. I know there are some tours, but I do not remember an exhibition being held in my constituency. If we are going to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars on new paintings

Supply-National Gallery I think the government should give consideration to arranging more extensive tours in all provinces, where many more people can see them.
Perhaps this particular expenditure is not going to be repeated, but if it is, I think the estimates for the national gallery should be referred either to one of the standing committees or to a select committee to be appointed. I do not like to see money being spent in such quantities without some kind of supervision. I hope the minister will give the matter consideration.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I must protest against this hill-billy approach to this particular question. I know that when it is in one item it sounds like a great deal of money, but we must remember that many organizations and many hon. members of this house have urged the government to build up a national gallery and national library in order to develop a cultural centre in Ottawa. I for one cannot see how anyone could reasonably protest at an investment of about six cents per capita in order to obtain a choice collection of world-known paintings.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not rise at this time to speak for the C.C.F., I am speaking for the people whom I represent in Selkirk. I think it is a shame that we should vote $885,000 for pictures. I have nothing against the finer arts but I had to work too hard when I was young to be able to participate in or enjoy them. I do not wish by any means to deprive other people of that pleasure, but in a booming economy such as we have here in 1956 we should be able to do something for poor people who have neither feed nor seed in the north of Selkirk constituency. I drew the attention of the Minister of Justice to the fact that this government had collected $300,000 from the people under the P.F.A.A. and they have not received any benefits in return.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Just let me go on for a couple of minutes and I will sit down. I want to go on and tell you what I have to say. I think it is a disgrace for the parliament of Canada to do that sort of thing today and now we are being asked to vote $885,000 for the finer arts when people are going hungry, when they have not the necessities of life. They do not know what to do and neither this government nor the provincial government will do a darn thing about it.
I appeal to the Prime Minister because he is the only man who smiles when I ask him. Mr. Prime Minister, please do something for these people because they are in terrible straits today.
(Mr. Thatcher.]

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister if any of this money is being spent to buy so-called abstract paintings. I attended an exhibition last year of what were called abstract paintings and I think they could have better been called a chamber of horrors. If we are spending money on such grotesque things as that, I think we might as well say-

speechtext: I remember that this item came before the estimates committee, that is, if I am correct in assuming that this item has nothing to do with the purchase of the Liechtenstein collection. Am I correct in that? Am I correct in assuming that this particular item of $885,000, or some of it at least, is in connection with the Liechtenstein collection?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
At that time,
when this matter came before the estimates committee, there was an attempt by some of the committee members to get some idea of the individual cost of the pictures. I do not think it was anybody's fault particularly that they could not get a very clear picture of it. The curator of the national gallery was not very well acquainted with the actual financial transactions, and as a consequence most of the members of the committee were, I think, left in doubt, as I was, as to the exact cost of that particular collection.
At that time I raised a question-not necessarily an objection but a question-as to the wisdom of devoting such large sums of money to the purchase of pictures from one particular school of painting of a very much earlier period. Whilst I recognize the necessity, if our gallery is really to assume the proportions of a representative art gallery, of having representatives of various schools of painting, I still thought that the fundamental purpose of our national gallery should be to establish, first of all, the world's outstanding collection of at least North American, if not of Canadian, paintings, and that we should be careful not to expend all

our funds on the collection of paintings that would constitute a selection very similar to those to be found in the other parts of the world.
I may say that when I raised that point in the estimates committee the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration listened to me with considerable sympathy, because, as he explained, I was speaking just the way his wife did almost every day on the matter. I think that we should perhaps question these purchases on some such basis as that. I agree, of course, that we have engaged art experts to make these purchases for us but, on the other hand, I think we should bear in mind the general social purpose of a national gallery, and I think that part of that social purpose is to put on display the various periods and developments of our own native painting, even though it might include some of the deplored abstract paintings that my hon. friend from Acadia mentioned just now. Whilst I also have great difficulty in comprehending abstract paintings when I see them, I am forced to the conclusion that there must be people of more discriminating taste than I who do find some satisfaction in them. I should think the gallery is not going to be complete in these days unless it does in its collection embody certain of these types of paintings.
I hope the minister, or possibly the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration when he comes with his main estimates, will be able to give us a more detailed account of the type of expenditure for which this money is being appropriated. Perhaps the Minister of Finance should tell us now, though, whether there is a certain level at which the national gallery seeks to leave funds at hand for the trustees to expend as they see fit. From the statements made last year, I rather gather there is some such item, but this appropriation this year seems to alter the picture in that regard.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
In connection with the commission paid on these paintings, I think the minister pointed out that it was five per cent on the first $400,000 and I believe it was four per cent on the balance. While not being familiar with the procedure in the buying of paintings, in a general sense it seems to me that the government and the national gallery, in making from time to time substantial purchases of paintings, could use some method whereby the taxpayers of Canada could be spared the inordinate amount of expense involved in commissions. If you are going to pay 5 per cent on the first $400,000, or the amount of $20,000, it seems to me that there are officials of the national gallery who should
Supply-National Gallery be able to negotiate purchases on behalf of the government at a great saving to the taxpayers.
There is one other matter with which I should like to deal. I should like the minister to inform the house just what percentage of paintings now owned by the national gallery are not on public view because of the lack of space and lack of facilities for showing them. It seems to me that I have heard many estimates of the numbers of paintings which are now stored away and which are inaccessible simply owing to the lack of sufficient space. If we are to be called upon to approve expenditures for the national gallery it seems to me that the government should be taking serious steps to make sure that when paintings are purchased, including all those which have been purchased in the past, they are made available at all times to the general public. There is not much point in having paintings if they are to be stored away down in the basement or in some place where they are not available to the citizens.
Then there is this other point which I think was raised by another hon. member. I think greater use should be made of the paintings in various parts of the country. While something has been done in this direction, I think perhaps more exhibitions in the principal centres throughout Canada would enable all Canada to get better value out of the money which we are appropriating at the present time.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
This item is for additional funds which are needed to finance the department because of acquiring further works of art. I am not objecting to the amount because if all of the facts were known I think the present government seems to be giving less recognition to the fine arts than is any other country in the world, including small countries. However, I am concerned about the veil of secrecy which seems to prevail in the matter of the purchase of these fine works of art. These paintings are being acquired by public funds for public enjoyment. I should like to know just what steps are being taken to protect the public, what process is being used in discovering the merits of certain valuations, and just what manner of protection is given to the public against fraudulent valuations. I do not think we have had enough information on that matter.
In the public accounts of Canada at page CC-24 the credit balance of the national gallery purchase account as of March 31, 1955 is in the amount of $425. That represents a decrease of $109,738.96 from the balance of $110,163.96 as of March 31, 1954. How many pieces of art were acquired during that time? I think the minister mentioned

Supply-National Gallery that a commission was paid. I should just like to know why a direct approach was not made in the matter of these purchases. Had the government taken that direct approach 1 think there would have been a considerable saving.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I am one of those who believe that our Canadian economy can afford a good living to the Canadian people and also supply us with some of the fine arts for the work of a good national gallery. I think it is a valuable asset to Canada. Apparently, from what has been said here, in some places we are not getting either. I think parliament should be concerned with what is to be obtained for that $885,000 or practically $1 million. I was reading over the committee report on the estimates last year. At that time when there was discussion about what the purchases would be, the item before the committee was for only some $130,000. On reading over the report it seemed to me that there were times when the committee was not given a satisfactory explanation as to the pictures which were being bought, the amounts which were being paid for them, the commissions that were being paid and the persons involved. I understand from the minister, however, that this $885,000 is for new purchases, or more recent purchases than the ones referred to in the estimates last year. If that is the case, I do not think parliament should pass these supplementary estimates until we have a statement in detail from the minister as to what these paintings are, how many paintings or pictures there are, who is receiving the commission for them and exactly what the item covers. In the estimates, as I see them here, there is certainly not sufficient explanation to cover that item. I should like to have a statement from the minister in that regard.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have been waiting to do that, of course, until all the other speeches were made. If there are any more, I shall have to wait further.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: I must confess that I know little about the procedure that is used in acquiring old masters. However, I should like to ask the minister just what the company or firm which got this $35,000 did to earn it? It is a considerable sum of money. One would wish to know just what services were given in return for this amount of money.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the art world I understand that there are agents comparable -if I may use such a mundane comparison -to real estate agents. But in this particular case it goes much further than that. Thomas Agnew and Sons Limited are an old and

respected agency in London for the handling of paintings and art treasures. Their reputation is such that, when they sell a picture, it is something that they have handled it and certified it from the standpoint of authenticity. In addition to that, it is the practice in the trade to pay a commission to the agent of the vendor. I would rather hope that the hon. member for Oxford would withdraw his amendment for that reason. This matter could have been gone into in some detail during last year's session when this department was before the estimates committee. I do not know whether or not it was gone into. But on every occasion when we have purchased paintings from this collection we have paid the commission. That is traditional and customary. With that, however, we get the advantage I have mentioned, namely that this firm with its reputation at stake is involved in the transaction to the point where they would not, in all probability, seek to sell to the national gallery of Canada something that might be questionable in the future.
The commissions are, I admit, negotiable in the sense that you do negotiate the commission but there is a range within which the settlements are made. The figures I have given you are not out of place for a $850,000 sale. For that reason we are obliged to pay it. If the amendment is carried, aside from whatever result it might have here, you destroy the sale, of course, because it is part of the transaction that we have agreed to go through with.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Am I correct in understanding the minister to say that this service that is supplied by the broker carries with it a guarantee that in the event of a picture turning out to be not authentic, the government might expect to be indemnified against loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: No. I did not mean to go that far and I carefully avoided doing so. I did not mean to misrepresent the matter at all. We do not get a written guarantee. On the other hand, this firm is one of the most reputable in the art world in London, England; and when you deal with them, you get something by way of assurance that they would not under any circumstances handle a picture about which there was any doubt in their minds.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: Can the minister say whether the Prince of Liechtenstein paid any commission for selling these pictures?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM

On the other hand, as I have said, there is a complete catalogue but we have not got room, as has been suggested here, to hang all these paintings at one time. However, that is not the purpose of a gallery. The purpose of a gallery is to provide showings from time to time of various kinds of art and various periods of art.
I can assure the hon. member for Acadia that there is no chamber of horrors. At least, I will put it this way, they are rather ancient compared with those about which he was thinking. There is one by Rubens, "The Entombment of Christ"; there is one by Simone Martini, called St. Catherine; there are two by Simeon Chardin, "The Governess" and "Returning from the Market". The first one is alleged to have been painted in 1615; the second was in 1320 and the last two were sometime in the eighteenth century. These are recognized works of art of some substance in the art world as well as in the financial world and they are being added to the collection in accordance with a policy which I think was begun four years ago when it became known that some of these paintings would be available.
I point out to hon. members that practically all the old masters are either in private hands or galleries in the United States or in Europe. You cannot buy them from national galleries. You can only buy this type of painting from a private owner -<nd there are very few private owners left.
Supply-National Gallery The Prince's collection is by long odds the largest single collection of this kind of art which is available for purchase and that is why the national gallery is taking the opportunity to buy these paintings. Perhaps this will be the only opportunity. I admit there is a question of Canadian art entering into this. Hon. members will recall that for the three or four years after the end of the war we were voting $100,000 a year for the purchase of art. I think it was then raised to $130,000 and that is the level at which it has continued. But you simply could not buy anything of this standard with money of that kind. It is for that reason these are extraordinary arrangements arrived at from time to time and brought forward as supple-mentaries, just at the time when the negotiations have been completed.
The hon. member for Prince Albert quite properly stressed the part that the national gallery would play in sustaining Canadian art, in the sense not only of purchasing some of it from time to time but putting it on exhibition. But you must remember that we do that. Quite a considerable sum of money has been expended on Canadian art, but Canadian art does not cost $885,000 for four pictures. It may be worth that some day and I sincerely hope it will. But one should not compare the amount of money spent. One should remember that these are almost priceless assets to the national gallery and naturally you are going to pay a good deal to get them.
On the other hand, I fully subscribe to the theory that at all times the director and board of trustees ought to be conscious of their responsibility to Canadian artists and to the Canadian public, in seeing that those paintings which have merit are given attention and shown at the proper time. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is an
item of $34,000 to provide for the expenses of

the royal commission on television and radio broadcasting. This is the royal commission the appointment of which was announced in December and whose sittings are to commence on April 30 next. The announcement that the government intended to appoint the royal commission-

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext: May I correct the hon. gentleman? The board of inquiry has been sitting and has been studying briefs, but the sittings that will be open to the public commence at the time he mentioned.

maintopic: BACON-SUGGESTED ATTEMPT TO NEGOTIATE CONTRACT WITH UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
I am referring to the public hearings. The royal commission has had certain private meetings as is known and they have invited the submission of briefs. They have announced publicly that they are going to commence their sittings on the 30th of April. It was on July 26 last that the government made the announcement of its intention to set up a royal commission, and in making that announcement the Minister of National Revenue said, as recorded on page 6875 of Hansard:
I am prepared to announce, on behalf of the government, that there will be either a commission or a board of inquiry set up some time within the near future to study the whole situation.
The "whole situation" embraces a great many problems that have been raised and were keenly debated last session in regard to radio and television policy in Canada. I do not think it can be said, when the government waited from July until December even to announce the setting up of the royal commission, that it moved very quickly. Nor can it be suggested that the royal commission has moved very quickly in commencing its public hearings only on the 30th of April.
The matters that have been referred to the royal commission are matters of high-indeed, I should say sweeping-importance in this field, and my personal regret is that the commission was not set up at a much earlier date than it was and that it has not found it possible to launch its hearings at a sufficiently early date to hold out some hope that its report might be available soon. Especially do I express that regret in view of one of the uses that the government has made in this house of the appointment of this royal commission. As hon. members will recall, on March 14 the government gave the appointment of the royal commission as a reason why it would not agree to the establishment this year of a committee of this house to review any aspect of policy or administration on the part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I have some observations to make in regard to this matter and also several associated

problems. So far as the attitude of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation toward the royal commission is concerned, it seems to me that the corporation ought to avoid saying or doing anything that is going to inject it into the realm of high policy in this regard. It seems to me that the proper view that the corporation should take of its responsibilities in this matter is that it should not be an advocate of any course of policy but should be merely the public servant which will carry out the policy that is decided upon. When it makes its submission to the royal commission I think it should be prepared-as I am sure it will be-to give to the royal ' commission all the information it requires and seeks. But I urge that it is not the function of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to be the advocate of any particular line of policy, having regard to the fact that it is a body responsible to parliament.
I raise this question specifically because it has come to my attention that the chairman of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in the course of an interview on the radio network, expressed some views that it seems to me could be interpreted-I do not say it was done deliberately for that purpose-in some quarters as calling upon organizations to rush forward and to make representations to the royal commission against any change in the present method of dealing with the licensing of broadcasting or television stations in Canada. I am the more concerned when I find that the text of the remarks made by Mr. Dunton in the course of the radio interview was published at the expense of the corporation-which means at the public expense-in the C.B.C. Times of March 11-17. This is the concluding paragraph. The question is this:
.	.	. what about the matter of licences and
regulations?
This question was put by Mr. Willis the interviewer. Mr. Dunton replied:
On this point there certainly have been quite a lot of differences of opinion. First of all I would like to point out that the C.B.C. doesn't set down its own responsibilities and powers, nor does it set the scale and shape of the development of broadcasting in Canada. These are all set by the Canadian people through their parliament. It is not for us to say what law should be or try to plead that it should be one way or the other, especially when a royal commission has just been set up to study the whole matter of broadcasting in Canada.
Here let me interject this remark. That last statement of Mr. Dunton seems to me to be a perfectly correct statement of the position that the corporation ought to take in relation to matters of policy and the royal commission. But Mr. Dunton went on to add this:
I would like to say this, though. The over-all broadcasting system that has grown up to serve 67509-159
Supply-Finance
Canada represents close and complex association of public and private enterprise, of commercial and public resources. Something is obviously needed to co-ordinate such a system under the difficult conditions set by the nature of Canada and under the various pulls and pressures coming from our great neighbouring country to the south. Where that responsibility for co-ordination should lie is for others to say. Indeed it is for the public and parliament to say if they do want the continuation of one over-all integrated system, or to split it into two or more different disintegrated systems, or to drop out one of the elements entirely and change the whole form of broadcasting in Canada. I think it would be too bad if, without people wanting it or realizing what was happening, the kind of integration we have was lost unconsciously through some change in the form of authority and responsibility, or if such a change led to duplication and confusion.
I think it would have been much more correct had Mr. Dunton paused where I paused this afternoon to offer my interjection. It is not the function of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in a matter of this kind, where a royal commission has been appointed by the government with the full approval of parliament, to inquire into such questions as Mr. Dunton is there referring to. I do not think Mr. Dunton should undertake to be making statements with regard to that matter.
I mention the use that the government has made in one particular, at any rate, of the fact that this royal commission is sitting. It used that fact as the excuse or pretext for denying the house the opportunity of considering this question, as has been the practice in times past, by a select committee of the house. An several other features of administration on the part of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation have been the subject of questions and, to a lesser extent, of answers, in the house at this session, I feel called upon to say a word about the responsibility of this house in relation to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
The corporation has traditionally taken the position that it is responsible to parliament. Parliament is called upon to vote money. At almost every session we are called upon to vote money. We were warned by the Minister of Finance on Tuesday evening in his budget speech, that we shall be called upon to vote moneys for the support of the corporation. Parliament votes these moneys on the recommendation of the government. Indeed it has no right, no authority or power to vote moneys for the support of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation without a recommendation by the governor in council. Under this system the government takes the responsibility of recommending and proposing to the house that sums be voted for the support of the corporation and its programs. The house therefore, it seems to me, has the right and duty to consider everything that

Supply-Finance
has a bearing on the administration of the corporation, including the use of public funds for programs.

That is the function of the government which is responsible to parliament. It is not the function of the head of any board, whether it be a board set up under a department and responsible to the minister of the department or a board directly responsible to parliament, to go out and declare policy. 558.	To provide for the destruction o£ harbour and gray seals-further amount required, $3,000.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: I just want to ask the minister a question regarding this item. I assume this is for the protection of the salmon fisheries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
There has been considerable complaint that the provision made for protecting the fisheries against the gray seals has been rather ineffective in the Atlantic region. To indicate the great loss that has been caused in the Atlantic salmon fisheries, I would cite the following figures. In 1954 there was produced 1,100,000 pounds; in 1955 this was reduced to 474,000 pounds. In Newfoundland and Labrador in 1954 it was 2,400,000 pounds; in 1955 it was 1,600,000 pounds. The people in the Atlantic provinces are becoming very much concerned with reference to their salmon fisheries, and it seems to me that this amount-I believe $35,000 was voted last year-is very small for this particular purpose.
It is also stated in some pamphlets I have received that each of these seals destroys something like 15,000 pounds of salmon in Northumberland straits and around the coast of New Brunswick. It is also stated, I think, that the method used to destroy the seals is not effective, and that the boats do not get near where the seals are and are not destroying them at the rate at which they should be destroyed.
I would suggest that this amount should be increased for this purpose. I realize that it cannot be increased in these supplementary estimates, but I thought this might be an appropriate time to bring up the matter, with the hope that there would be some increase in the amount of money that is used for destroying those seals, which are one of the chief reasons the Atlantic salmon fisheries are being depleted at the present time.

The minister has not answered my question. I wanted to know whether this money was being used in the Atlantic provinces principally for the destruction of seals, or where it was being used.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: I must apologize to my bon. friend. This is used both in the Atlantic and Pacific areas. During the current year the $35,000 has run to an almost even $17,000 in the Atlantic-Newfoundland area and $18,000 in the Pacific area. The $3,000 is going to be spent in about the same proportions. As to increasing the vote, of course the bounty is paid on the number of seals that are killed at $10 an adult and $5 a pup. Presumably if more seals were killed we would pay a larger bounty and would vote a larger sum.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: Is the money used entirely for bounty, or is it used also for destroying the seals?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF FISHERIES
speechtext: No. It is a bounty paid to those who kill the seals.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: NATIONAL FILM BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take just a moment to call to the attention of the government a suggestion that was made recently in the Saskatchewan legislature by Hon. C. C. Williams. The suggestion was that we are in a complicated1 situation in Canada because of the large number of boards of film censors that we have, and it might be a good idea to try to reduce the number. Mr. Williams' suggestion was that there might be two such boards, one in eastern Canada and one in western Canada, so there might be more co-ordination and cohesion in this work.
I recognize right away, before someone from the government side starts to tell me, that this is not something that can be done by direction, from the federal government. It is something that would have to come about by way of co-operation among the provinces concerned. But it does seem to me that the national film board, which is in this field, might take a lead in furthering Mr. William's suggestion. That is all I wish to do at this time, Mr. Chairman, just to draw to the attention of the government and of the national film board this matter, in the hope that they will give consideration to it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT
speechtext: This is real property. Might I add something more. The purpose of this vote is, as my hon. friend has seen, to deal with a situation that arises because we had not covered it in the original St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act. These lands, having been made available for disposal, went to Crown Assets Disposal Corporation, which only has authority to pay the proceeds of any sale into the consolidated revenue fund, and it was not the intention to do that here. It was the intention rather that this money should be part of the St. Lawrence seaway authority fund, so this is a vote to put it back there. In order to overcome this situation in the future an amendment is going to be made to the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority Act to provide that they may dispose of their own assets and keep the proceeds for their capital account.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who adjourned the debate does not seem to be here; I do not know whether he is going on or not. I shall be only a moment. There are a few things I should like to suggest to the parliamentary assistant in connection with this bill. The parliamentary assistant, being a member of the legal profession, will understand and appreciate that some of the complaints I offer probably can be rectified.
The first one I should like to suggest to him is that in the whole matter of obtaining a loan under this legislation there is too much red tape from the day you start to the day you finish. The parliamentary assistant is no doubt familiar with the application form, which should certainly take the prize for being the most complicated and complete form that anybody has ever been asked to fill out. I would suggest to him that something be done to simplify the application form.
Other hon. members have mentioned that there should be more offices in eastern Ontario. I think the parliamentary assistant will agree that there have been fairly few applications under this legislation. One of the reasons for that, apart from the red tape, is that the office is situated in Toronto.
I should like to impress upon the parliamentary assistant the fact that in the matter of the evaluation, not too much attention should be paid to the municipal assessments. It is quite true that in the last two or three years there have been reassessments in many counties, but he knows, and as all other members of the legal profession know, the assessment of property in many instances has little relation to the real value of the property.

I would suggest to the parliamentary assistant that the evaluator or appraiser pay a great deal more attention to the individual himself who is making the application, to his background, to his character, and to what he has been able to do in farming in the past.
Canadian Farm Loan Act
I do not want to repeat all the other suggestions that have been made to the parliamentary assistant except one, and that is that the percentage of the loan could and should be increased to 75 per cent. He is quite aware of the amounts that are lent under the Veterans' Land Act, under the Central Mortgage and Housing Act, and also under the act administered by the province of Ontario.
If the parliamentary assistant would do something to see that the red tape in the application form is eliminated, that evaluations are speeded up, and that something is done about the members of his own profession who handle these loans, it would be a great help. I know the blame is generally placed on the lawyer, which not always is the case. I have found that in many cases before the loan is completed the applicant is very much annoyed, and in many instances wishes that he had never bothered to make the application in the first place.
As far as the rate of interest is concerned, I would suggest to the parliamentary assistant that surely this government could well follow the example of Ontario and make money available at 4 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, before you put the motion I would like to make a few comments. The bill proposes to make some changes which I hope will be beneficial to the farmers. I hope they will be able to get loans put through with a little less red tape. I believe some of the methods used by the department should be changed. For instance, I know of a case where a farmer made an application for a loan and this is the reply he received from the Canadian farm loan board:
Your preliminary application for a loan from this board has been carefully reviewed.
As the amount you require on the security offered is very much in excess of what the board may be able to lend, it appears that we are unable to be of assistance to you at this time.
I consider that an extremely abrupt refusal. I think the board should have some method worked out under which they could have said that in this case the greatest amount of money that could be loaned was such and such. This method would give the farmer an idea of how much he could borrow, and he could then make another application.
My request at this time is that some of the red tape be done away with, and that some of the methods currently used in turning down an application for a loan without giving the applicant any indication of what he could borrow should be changed. I think such a policy as is presently in operation is not in the best interests of either the farmers themselves or of the operation of the act.

Canadian Farm Loan Act
Mr. John Pallet! (Peel):	Mr. Speaker,
before the bill goes to the committee I would like to address a few words in respect to some of the amendments which have been introduced.
I wonder what the purpose of the farm loan bill is at the present time. Is it to give agriculture some sort of an impetus, or is it to say that the government has done something for the farmers, or is it merely to waste our time in this house through introducing this measure? The reason I suggest that is because the amendments which have been offered are extremely insignificant, and the increases are of no consequence.
In leaving the interest rate at 5 per cent we have an indication that the government is not able to handle money as efficiently as other institutions in this country. I wonder if the parliamentary assistant or the minister could tell us the spread in the cost of the money they are lending to the farmer. The question I asked concerns the rate you are paying for the money you are lending at 5 per cent. I am leaving that question in order that an answer may be given at some future date.
Another point I would like to mention is that you have here an arbitrary valuation for the farm loan. I know that in the amendment to the Industrial Development Bank Act there is no arbitrary figure for valuation as there is for farm loans. Is this a form of discrimination between industry and agriculture? Are we going to encourage young people in this country to go on farms and develop that industry by not leaving some flexibility in the assessing of one farm against another, or are they to be treated exactly the same? You have a discriminatory clause in the Industrial Development Bank Act. I suggest there is a different approach here. Shall we give industry as much as they want within certain limits, as far as valuation is concerned, but not as to the percentage of the loan, whereas if a farmer wants a loan he is to be bound by the hard and fast limits of the valuation?
Other hon. members have already suggested that another comparison may be drawn by

reference to the limits of the National Housing Act. There is a much higher lending value under that act, and again we have a discriminatory factor. Agriculture is in a position today which does not compare favourably with other industries in the country. The government comes forward with an amendment to an act that could assist the farmer, yet the government is not brave enough, shall I say, to make the amendment something with teeth in it.
If we are going to keep our young people on the farm, Mr. Speaker, we will have to give them some encouragement. Apart from the other problems which face these young people there is a problem which is particularly peculiar to agriculture. I am referring to the necessity of refinancing every 20 years. Statistics now show, and have shown for some time, that the average farm in this country is refinanced every 20 years. That is not the case in industry or in any other type of business. If we are going to keep young people on the farm, and if we are going to preserve the industry which has been of such benefit to this country, we have a responsibility to approach it on that basis.
I close my remarks, Mr. Speaker, by saying that the lending possibilities under this act are too restrictive, and that in comparing it with the National Housing Act and the Industrial Development Bank Act there appears to be considerable discrimination against the farmer in the government's approach to the handling of money.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think this matter was adequately dealt with at the resolution stage, and as it is going to the banking and commerce committee I shall not have more than a word or two to say at this time. I am particularly glad that this bill is going to that committee, because I think there are certain things which need to be explored a bit and upon which we should be enlightened.
I was very surprised to find, as a kind of offshoot of the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines proposal, that the well known Mr. Murchison explained that he had asked the industrial development bank to commit itself for $70 million in securities. I do not suppose he found his way in there entirely on his own, and I confess I was surprised that that had even been contemplated. I shall be interested to learn more about it.
Furthermore, I think it is important for us to explore in greater detail the relationship between the chartered banks and the industrial development bank. The theory is that the industrial development bank steps in only where the other banks have stepped out. I think we might well have further information as to just exactly what is meant by other banks stepping out, whether perhaps they do it under suggestion. At any rate I do not propose to take up any more time because these matters can be discussed better in the committee.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill to extend the lending field of the government's industrial development bank is to be sent to the committee on banking and commerce for further examination. Therefore I shall make my remarks with as much brevity as possible, in the hope that when the bill reaches the committee stage some of my principal observations will
22. 1956	2515
Industrial Development Bank Act be gone into thoroughly along with other critical remarks made by previous speakers, and thus help to eliminate some of the unfavourable aspects of the lending policy of the industrial development bank.
I was pleased to see the general view held by those who spoke during the resolution stage of this legislation, when they emphasized the initial purpose of the bank, namely to facilitate and make more easily available loans for the little enterpriser. I am in full agreement with that, because it seems to me that it is the little enterpriser in our country who needs help at the present time. The big fellows seem to be doing all right. I am thinking of the financial dilemma faced by many businessmen in this country when they make application to the chartered banks, the insurance companies or other commercial agencies for long-term loans at reasonable rates. In most cases they are discouraged and are unable to obtain loans.
The result is that many of our small businesses in this country are unable to expand, are unable to acquire necessary premises, are unable to replace obsolete machinery with new equipment and generally to streamline their activities in order to meet competition from the big corporations. Such expansion is necessary for the little Canadian businessman if he is to survive. The only way he can survive is to match competition by the giant corporations.
Since the opening of parliament on January 10 a variety of subjects have been discussed and just about every segment of our community has been involved. A few minutes ago hon. members quite properly indicated the difficulties of the farmer and urged policies that would alleviate some of his troubles. On previous occasions hon. members have referred to the difficulties which face labour as a consequence of being unemployed. A few days ago the house was in debate on a resolution with respect to inducing heavy industry to locate in depressed areas of our country. However, very little reference has been made to the man who constitutes the majority of the commercial units in our country, the small independent Canadian businessman, in connection with the loaning facilities of the industrial development bank. I think it is proper for us to focus attention upon that little businessman, because he certainly is deserving of attention at this time.
It seems to me that there are two obstacles which face the small Canadian businessman. The first is the taxation policy of this country, which places an extremely heavy burden on him, which strikes at him much harder than it strikes at the large corporations which

Industrial Development Bank Act have access to long-term loans at reasonable rates of interest or which can float stock issues to finance their needs.
Another obstacle is the fact that the little businessman is unable to float long-term loans at reasonable interest rates in order to finance his expansion and at the same time sustain himself when credit and instalment buying are the fashion as they are at this time. I have discussed this problem with many of the small businessmen in my community, and I have found that while they have been able to perfect their skills, while they have been able to invite new business, while they have been able to establish themselves in the community and provide necessary services, invariably they have had difficulty in obtaining sufficient money to bring about the expansion needed to meet new business. As I indicated before, the large corporations are able to do this.
Under present circumstances, in the case of the little businessman one of three things is bound to happen to him. He becomes discouraged and goes out of business, he becomes stagnant, or he loses his independence. By losing his independence I mean that he succumbs to the various inducements held out to him by the giant corporations, and eventually a merger results. I do not think that that is a healthy thing because if we eliminate the little Canadian businessman from our midst we eliminate the most important factor which provides the competitive atmosphere required in our economic life.
Naturally the proper step would be to bring about a certain amount of tax exemption. The Minister of Finance knows very well that the little Canadian businessman is taxed twice, first as a corporate body and then in the form of personal income tax. I submit that the main policy of the industrial development bank should be to indicate that it has a little more confidence in our small businessmen and their enterprises. As I say, if we eliminate the small businessman from our midst there will be in the future serious implications, both in the social and economic sense.
As I understand it, one change to be made is to increase the amount available for loans of over $200,000 from $50 million to $75 million. We must realize that the influx of United States capital during the last ten years has been very heavy, the yearly average being close to $400 million. Therefore it is quite obvious that we should give preference and some sort of inducement to Canadians to invest in Canada.
In addition we should recall that during the post-war years over $4,000 million has
I Mr. Holowach.]

been provided to help economies outside of Canada. No one is criticizing the wisdom of our having done that; we did it voluntarily and I think part of that program has been most successful, but it is strange that our government should be so inept in giving this treatment to our own small Canadian businessman.
I am not interested in the applicant who is thinking in terms of a loan of over $200,000, but I am very concerned that priority should be given to the little Canadian businessman who requires a much more modest accommodation, not to get rich in a hurry but to sustain himself in our economic life.
We should consider the trend that is taking place today, and there is statistical evidence to prove that this is a fact. Big business is becoming bigger while the little merchant, the little retailer, the wholesaler, the little processor, is becoming smaller all the time. If that trend continues then I submit that in the next 25 years the little Canadian businessman might well be completely eliminated from our midst. As I stressed before, if we allow that to happen there will be serious implications involved as far as our social and economic structures are concerned. I once again urge that in the matter of lending policy the industrial development bank give high priority to the little Canadian businessman.
There is one more point I wish to emphasize, and that is the need of setting up more offices across Canada in connection with the activities of the industrial development bank, not only in those areas which are developed or undergoing development but particularly in those areas which are underdeveloped. I certainly would like to see also some representation in the province of Alberta.
In concluding, let me say that I think we should do everything we possibly can to induce Canadians to invest in Canada, and a good start would be for the industrial development bank to give incentive to the little Canadian businessman to invest in his own enterprise and in his own country. If we think this matter through carefully I am sure we shall realize that we cannot sustain a healthy prosperity unless we look after him.

speechtext:
I should like to emphasize again one of the points I raised at an earlier stage on this measure. Now that I have seen the bill I realize that what I had hoped might be done is apparently not going to be done. I note that the measure we have before us proposes to widen the areas in which the industrial development bank may make loans. I presume that means that the government considers that those particular fields are fields

in which we require an expanded investment, and it wishes to make that investment more readily available to those wishing to enter those fields.
I am going to suggest that it is not sufficient merely to widen the scope of the bank in this way if we are not at the same time going to widen its capacity to enter that field. I believe that the industrial development bank offers us an opportunity to undertake something that we are going to have to do sooner or later in this country, and that is to direct as well as we can the flow of investment into those areas which in the consideration of this parliament are the areas in which the Canadian economy requires development.
I imagine that a great many hon. members listened yesterday, as I did, to Mr. James Duncan, the president of Massey Harris, speaking to a meeting in Ottawa on his recent experiences in the Soviet union. Like me, they must have been impressed with Mr. Duncan's report of the vigour with which the Russian regime and the Russian people were pursuing a policy of carefully considered economic development. They were, according to Mr. Duncan, directing their efforts to development in those fields in which the Russian regime considered the Russian economy required development.
They, of course, are doing it there with a particularly ruthless hand and without any regard whatever for the individual comforts or desires of the Russian people, at least, not further than they require to attend to those desires and wishes. But it is becoming increasingly evident that it is this carefully designed and carefully controlled flow of investment in the Soviet union that has created the menace, economically, which now confronts the western world.
If we are going to meet that menace, if we are going to be able to compete in the world for the survival of our political and social ideas, then we are going to have to meet them in the economic field. I suggest that the industrial development bank, an instrument that has already been developed in this country, could have its scope very much widened and could accomplish that end. At the present time, of course, it is severely limited by the fact that its total assets for lending do not exceed $100 million; $25 million in capital and the power to issue debentures for an additional $75 million. A $100 million investment is not a very large item in the sort of economy that was described to us the other night by the Minister of Finance.
I should hope that the government would see fit, if not this session then in the next session, to consider seriously making the
22, 1956	2517
Industrial Development Bank Act industrial development bank a deliberate instrument for the direction of investment in the Canadian economy. I noticed, for instance, in the papers the Minister of Finance tabled before his budget speech, the figures were given for the increased disbursements in the different sectors of our economy. He reported that the corporation investment income in Canada had increased last year to, I believe, some $756 million.
One of the complaints that have been made both in this house and outside this house by people who should know-people such as Mr. Coyne, the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. James Muir, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada and many other leading industrialists and financiers in Canada-has been that the Canadian investor by and large is not particularly interested in moving into the more venturesome fields of investment and that he has, on the other hand, tended to invest in safe, fixed-yield investments rather than take the risks in developmental types of investment, with the consequence that we have had the vast inflow of foreign capital into those fields of investment.
Whilst we may take the position that investment of this sort from any source does have the effect of developing our Canadian economy, we should bear in mind that it has the effect of removing completely from the control of the Canadian parliament the fields in which our economy is going to expand. I would suggest that, since the Canadian investor appears to be a rather cautious soul, we might meet his cautious desires for safe investment by providing the opportunity in the form of very little expanded debenture issues of the bank of industrial development, which would then be available for investment in the areas of our economy that are now virtually a foreign preserve.
Before this measure goes through the house I hope there will be an opportunity for the government to reconsider the rather restricted increase in the powers of the bank proposed in this measure, and to take some steps toward making it an instrument of investment direction in our economy.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have only a few remarks to make on second reading of the bill to amend the Industrial Development Bank Act. The first is that I am pleased to see that the amending bill indicates that the scope of operations of the bank is to be enlarged. I would suggest for the minister's consideration that the scope be enlarged a little bit further. Industrial development in Canada is going into fields which are not yet covered in the Industrial Development Bank Act and which may well need certain large-scale assistance.
In my own county of Peel we are much concerned with the specialized types of agriculture. I suggest that the development of agriculture in that county, in certain types of crops such as fruit, vegetables and indoor crops, is actually approaching the development stage of a small industry. Even individual farms must be capitalized on a large scale. The machinery required for their operation is extensive. They cannot be dealt with properly under the farm loan acts, on the capitalization set out in those acts. They are progressing from the stage of family farms to that of more commercial enterprises.
Two sessions ago, Mr. Speaker, in the debate that took place with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), I recall that he said that in some provinces of Canada farming was a way of life but in Ontario it was an industry. Referring to those words of his, I would suggest that we who are giving second reading to the bill amending the Industrial Development Bank Act recognize that progress and enlarge the scope of this act to include agriculture. I would suggest that we recognize the much larger capitalization required today by young people to get into agriculture, and at the same time recognize the fact that agriculture is becoming more scientific and in many ways more nearly based on the industrial approach.


I note with interest and without further comment that in the act which is before us there- is no specific provision concerning the amount of interest that may be charged. I suppose that each individual loan is negotiated on its own basis. If there is good security the bank might possibly advance loans at a low interest rate, whereas if the loan is not so well secured the interest rate might be higher.
One feature of the operation of the industrial development bank that I am pleased to note is shown on the annual report to the Minister of Finance for 1955 at page 11. There we find that the revenue for the year ended September 30, 1955, is up over that of the year previous by $98,684, and that the bank has managed to decrease its operating expenses by $10,212. In those figures I suggest there is a good lesson for government. They show that this bank, operating on a business basis, can show a profit, can increase revenues and decrease expenses. Here is an example that might perhaps be followed by all branches of government, through adopting the system followed by the bank by means of which they have managed to decrease expenses in this year of expanding government expenses.
One other suggestion that I desire to make for the consideration of the minister and the house is that in industrial expansion there is a problem that was faced a few years ago in connection with housing expansion. In order to find accommodation, industry must resort to new sources of capital. People who could not afford to build their own homes were allowed to rent apartments. Those apartments were financed under the National Housing Act. I suggest that the same situation faces many small industries today. They have not the equity capital with which to furnish their machinery, keep available the necessary working capital and at the same time purchase a new factory. Today in Canada there is a shortage of money for people who would be prepared to invest some equity in a factory and make it available to an operating business of some sort on a rental basis.
To you, Mr. Speaker, and to this house I suggest that steps might be taken under this act whereby people who are prepared to build factories to enlarge the industrial capacity of this country, and to rent those factories to industries, might be able to borrow money under provisions similar to those at present provided for housing under the National Housing Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall speak for only a few minutes in connection with second reading of this bill, because I feel that at the resolution stage I expressed my views on as wide a basis as

possible. There are, however, a couple of observations that I should like to make and I shall avoid, if at all possible, repeating what I said on the previous occasion.
I believe there are a few matters which might be considered by the committee upon reference of this bill to them. One of the things that it seems to me will be required for the effective broadening of the scope of the work of this institution is the opening of additional offices of the bank in more centres in Canada. We referred to that matter previously. Apparently there are only four regional offices. If we are going to make this type of money available to smaller business institutions, we must get down to their level. I would hope that the committee might give serious consideration to a recommendation of that kind when it is considering this bill.
The second thing I want to mention is this. The additional funds that are being made available, it appears, are to be limited to those institutions which require loans of $200,000 or more. An institution of that type can ordinarily go into the bond market, through the usual financial institutions, and obtain the kind of money it needs. I would think that what the country needs is an expansion of funds for those institutions which require help between the help that can be given to them by ordinary banking methods and the help they can obtain in the bond market. I would suggest that more consideration might be given to this phase of the bank's activities.
I note with satisfaction one particular point, and that is that officers of the bank may be delegated considerably more power than they have had in the past. I understand that the supervisor for the whole of the Ontario area has discretionary power up to $5,000, but otherwise all applications made to him must be referred to the head office of the bank in Montreal. If we are going to have this type of business get down to the level I have spoken about, then obviously we shall have to have greater responsibility and greater authority placed in the hands of the people who actually deal with the applicants.
At this stage, too, before we embark on this type of endeavour on a grand scale, it might be wise if the committee to which this measure is to be referred called in representatives of the chartered banks to see if, in fact, those institutions might not be interested in expanding their activities in this field. You will recall that at one stage those institutions were not interested in loans under Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. However, when the necessary legislation was enacted by this house they lost little time in getting into the field in a big way. Although there
22, 1956	2519
Farm Improvement Loans Act may have been some reluctance at one time about being involved in this field, it seems to me that before it is expanded on too large a scale we ought to hear evidence as to whether those institutions might see their way clear to provide funds on this type of security.
If that should not be the case, sir, then I say there is going to be a great deal more money required by this industrial development bank if it is going to perform its proper function. I was very interested to hear the president of Canadian National Railways say that the $500 million program of that company spread over the last four years and the year to come has been financed entirely through Canadian bond houses. We are pleased, Mr. Chairman, to support this resolution providing for the extension of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. We believe this is an excellent example of the type of system that should be used and could be used to provide loans to needy borrowers, good farmers, at a reasonable rate of interest. The act has now been in operation since 1945, and up to the end of 1954 loans had been made totalling more than $513 million. The government provides a guarantee of 10 per cent of the aggregate loans granted by the banks; therefore the total amount guaranteed in this period amounted to over $50 million. In spite of the very large guarantee, and in spite of the very large sums of money lent under this act, the losses in that period amounted to less than $150,000. The government's experience in this field, therefore, has been excellent. Within this period the government suffered a loss of only one three hundred and fiftieth of the guarantee involved.
I believe the government should consider adopting this type of practice in connection with other legislation. Here is a method the government uses in co-operation with the banks, and with a guarantee of only 10 per cent it has facilitated the making of many loans. I suggest that the experience of the government with respect to this act to date has been very happy. I am pleased that once again when this act is being extended the amount of the guarantee of a loan to an individual applicant is once again increased.


The last time the act was before parliament the amount was increased from $3,000 to $4,000. This time it is being increased from $4,000 to $5,000. I think the government might have increased that amount even further.
There has been a tremendous increase in the cost of the things farmers buy for which they obtain money under this act. The item that farmers have to purchase most frequently is farm machinery. As hon. members know, there have been tremendous increases in the prices of farm machinery. Knowing the amount of farm machinery, to say nothing of other improvements, that may be needed on a modern farm, I think the government might have allowed the ceiling for which a guarantee would be applicable to be considerably above the suggested $5,000 figure. I think it is generally agreed that an efficient farm today needs machinery to the value of about $20,000. I would suggest that as far as the ceiling on the individual loan is concerned, the guarantee might well have been doubled and applied to a maximum of $8,000.
There is one further suggestion I should like to make to the minister. I know he has already given some consideration to this matter. I hope he will call in the credit unions at an early date, and that the role they may be able to play under an act such as this will be actively considered. I hope the government will give favourable consideration, as I am sure it will, to co-operating with the credit unions in this field in so far as the credit unions themselves may request and within the terms of the legislation itself.
As has been pointed out in the past, the number of credit unions has increased very rapidly. Some 1,600,000 Canadians are members of credit unions. We believe that credit unions, and the whole idea of credit unions, should be encouraged by the government. What has actually happened in practice in credit unions in the making of farm improvement loans has very frequently been this. A farmer has gone to a bank and applied for a loan under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and for one reason or another the bank has turned him down. The farmer, following the rejection by the bank manager, has gone to a credit union, made an application for a loan, and very frequently has received a loan from the credit union for the same purpose. The records of the credit unions in regard to loans for farm machinery and farm improvements will show that their losses have been very small, in spite of the fact that the loans the credit unions have made in general have been loans that would entail a greater risk than similar loans made by the banks.

I am hopeful that before the end of this session the government, by new legislation or by regulation, may extend this act to credit unions so the full 10 per cent guarantee may be given to credit unions and that farmers generally will be able to take greater advantage of this method of obtaining loans at a reasonable rate, namely 5 per cent.
I want to point out again that this is a method by which borrowers can obtain loans at a reasonable rate of interest, and I hope the government will expand this type of legislation so that the very high rates of interest now charged by some other lending institutions in this country may be reduced from the very high rate of over 24 per cent to as little as possible, with the ultimate objective of getting the rate down to the same level provided for in this type of legislation.
