speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Trans-
Canada Highway Act, which became law on December 10, 1949, was enacted to encourage and assist in the construction of a continuous high standard highway following the shortest practical east-west route across Canada. The act provides that the federal government may make contributions to a provincial government of 50 per cent of the construction costs of the highway over a period of seven years, and the agreements under the act provide further that the federal government may pay in respect of highway previously constructed along the route of the trans-Canada highway between April 1, 1928 and December 10, 1949. The estimated cost of completing the highway was $300 million in 1949, and the amount voted by parliament as the federal government share was $150 million.
The total length of the highway along the designated route in all ten provinces is approximately 5,000 miles. Quebec has not signed an agreement under the statute and has not participated. The mileage in the nine participating provinces, including Banff and Yoho national parks, is 4,580 miles.
For distances totalling approximately 2,850 miles there is a paved highway, although to date the equivalent of only 1,600 miles have been constructed to the approved standard. Thus there remain approximately 1,545 miles of highway unpaved, and there are 185 miles on which there is no highway of any kind.
It is therefore now apparent that the terms of the present agreements, which provide for the completion of the project by December 9, 1956, cannot be met. There have been various reasons for delays, including weather, the necessity of diverting materials and effort into the defence build-up at the time of the Korean war, difficult terrain and others. In the over-all, however, progress has been disappointingly slow.
The purpose of this amendment is to seek authority to introduce a bill to extend the period of construction, to provide additional funds, and to alter the formula so as to enable the federal government to provide greater


financial assistance in constructing select sections with a view to closing at the earliest possible date those gaps in which no highway exists at all at the present time, or in which there is a road of inferior standard which needs to be rebuilt.
In no province does the gap or the combined lengths of gaps where there is no highway of any kind exceed 10 per cent of the total mileage in that province. The resolution therefore indicates that the bill will seek authority for the Minister of Finance to pay a higher contribution for a portion of the highway in a province not exceeding 10 per cent of the mileage. The federal government contribution for these gaps will be increased from 50 per cent to 90 per cent of the cost of construction.
The resolution also refers to the extended period for which contributions may be made. The present terminating date, as I have indicated, is December 9, 1956. The bill will seek authority to extend the period for construction to December 31, 1960, and a further five months to wind up the accounting. The termination date for all contributions therefore will be set as May 31, 1961.
The last financial provision which is set forth in the resolution has to do with the total amount of money authorized by parliament for federal contributions. As I have already indicated and as the committee is aware, the limitation in the present statute is $150 million. Authority will be sought in the bill to increase this amount to a maximum of $250 million.

The amount of traffic travelling on our roads has also increased, and the life of the roads is shortened. The sum of $150 million was spent on the construction of roads with a 22-foot top. speechtext:
For the gaps that are left,
I suppose. This little book says it is 10 per cent of the distances that are left in each of the provinces. Therefore the government is going to pay 90 per cent of the 10 per cent gaps that are left. I suggest that this government should pay 90 per cent of the cost of the construction of the whole road. As I understand it the dominion government has not the machinery or the ways and means for the building of roads and therefore they place the responsibility upon the provinces. But this is a national road and it should be built, not 10 per cent of the gap but all the gap, by this federal government at least to the extent of 90 per cent.
Then there is the matter of maintenance. It is estimated that this road will be completed in 1961, but I have my doubts. Some of these gaps are to be found in the most rugged country, and much of the trans-Canada highway is going to be worn out before it is completed, especially the 22-foot portions. This road should be built to a minimum width of 30 feet, and where the traific is heavy it should be at least a four-lane highway.
You are asking the provinces to pay 50 per cent, and they also receive 50 per cent on the 67509-160

Trans-Canada Highway Act old highways that are used or included in the national highway. It must be remembered that this is practically the only road in Canada to which the dominion government contributes one iota. Last year a total of $600 million was spent on highways in Canada, $426 million of which was spent by the provinces, $110 million by the municipalities and a measly $27 million by the federal government. About $17 million of that was in connection with the trans-Canada highway, with the balance presumably being spent on roads in national parks.
Highway traffic is increasing at a terrific rate, the number of cars having almost doubled in the last six years, as well as the number of trucks. The provinces are faced with a problem in keeping up their highway systems, especially if the present traffic trend should continue. The province of Ontario is hemmed in almost like a horseshoe by the United States, and it must have good roads. Good roads are necessary for defence purposes. In case of emergency the people of the cities of Ontario are not going to go east and west; they are not going to go south to the United States. Most of them are going to go north. It is fortunate that we have a great tourist development in Haliburton and Victoria which could take care of many people in case of an emergency. We must have good commercial and tourist roads running north and south, not only in Ontario but in many other provinces. The provinces are hard pressed to find money with which to build these north and south roads. It is more important today to have north and south roads than it is to have east and west roads, because such roads are necessary for commercial and tourist purposes as well as for national and civil defence. There must be good roads to places like Sarnia, Detroit, Windsor, London, the Niagara district, Hamilton, Toronto, and do not forget Port Hope where our great uranium centre is located. Then there are the cities and towns and bridges along the St. Lawrence. The same applies to Quebec, and that is probably one reason Quebec did not come into this national highway scheme.
However, this is like a man who is hungry; half a loaf is better than no bread at all. I do not think the dominion government has an excuse in the world for not paying 90 per cent both of the cost of construction and the cost of maintenance. They will have to start maintaining some of it long before the last of the road is built. This government retains about 78 cents of every tax dollar collected

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, back in 1949 when the government introduced a resolution designed to assist the provinces financially in the construction of Canada's first national highway, I am sure those who voted for the legislation and Canadians generally felt that at long last the federal government had accepted its responsibility for the construction of an integrated system of highways in this country, and had acknowledged that it was absolutely necessary that the government take this step. I am sure Canadians thought that the commencement of the trans-Canada highway was the first step toward the realization of a system of integrated highways across this country.
Seven years have passed since the introduction of that legislation, legislation which Canadians thought would usher in a new era in motor transportation in this country. As has been mentioned already by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Public

Trans-Canada Highway Act
I think what I have said sums up briefly a few of the reasons why we believe the federal government must accept, in greater measure than anything we have seen heretofore, its responsibility in connection with a highway program. After all, the magnitude of the job which the provinces are obliged to do to maintain the farm-to-market roads as well as the highways places them, as I said a moment ago, in an impossible position, and one which they are not going to be able to maintain in the future unless some assistance is forthcoming from the federal government.
What has happened to account for the fact that the present trans-Canada highway program has not become the success that it was hoped it would be by those who introduced it? There are several reasons. First and possibly most important is the fact that the 50-50 sharing of costs between the federal government and the provincial governments was not by any stretch of the imagination a realistic division of costs. It did not take into consideration the purchase of land for the right of way, nor did it take into consideration the substantial costs involved in moving telephone poles and many of the other obstacles the government found in many cases when they laid out the right of way. When you take into consideration the extra costs, instead of there being a 50-50 sharing of cost we find it is more in the neighbourhood of 40-60, with the provinces being responsible for the 60 per cent rather than the 40 per cent.
Another regressive feature was that the provinces were responsible for any clover-leafs that had to be built, and any overpasses that were necessary on the route. These two features are items of great expenditure. In so far as the provinces going ahead at a faster rate than they did is concerned, possibly one of the restraining factors was the fact I mentioned a moment ago, namely that they are responsible for their roads within their own boundaries. Everyone knows it is absolutely necessary that the provinces maintain and build to the best of their ability the roads which the people within the boundaries of each province necessarily are obliged to use for their day to day living. Increased construction costs have also added to the burden. Hence a combination of a great many factors has been the cause which appears to have retarded the construction of the trans-Canada highway.
As I pointed out, the amendment with which we are dealing this evening is not going to help this situation materially, because the 90 per cent the federal government is prepared to pay on 10 per cent of the total mileage within each province in effect amounts to only 4 per cent or 5 per cent of fMr. Bryson.]
the total cost of the trans-Canada highway. When we take the new proposal and add it to the original proposal of the 50-50 break in cost sharing, and when we take into consideration the fact that the provinces are responsibile for the things I mentioned a moment ago, we find that the breakdown in reality is still only 50-50 in so far as sharing of costs is concerned, and that is not enough.
The hon. member who just took his seat said this new proposal will end, in so far as the latest statement we have is concerned, in 1961 and he doubted whether the road would be completed by that date. I also doubt very much whether it will be completed then. I think we must remember that the job which must be done in British Columbia, for instance-the fabulous and fantastic job that the provincial government of British Columbia is facing today-makes it appear extremely unlikely that they will have their portion of the highway completed by 1961. Of course we also know that the terms of the proposal are that the money will be forthcoming, under the new terms, provided that each province allocates each year as much money as the average they have allocated in the last two years in connection with the ordinary construction of the road.
While I am not going to deal with the situation as we find it in the United States in so far as cost sharing is concerned between the federal government and the state governments, it is interesting to note that the federal government of the United States assists in the building and maintenance of all the roads in that country. Last year it budgeted for something in the neighbourhood of $700 million to help build and maintain a comprehensive road grid in that country. Hence we are somewhat disappointed that the new proposal that has been made is not going far enough.
We would suggest that an announcement should be made now as to what are plans of the federal government for when the trans-Canada highway is completed in the provinces. For instance, what is going to happen or what is the program going to be in the province of Manitoba, or the province of Ontario or the province of Saskatchewan when they complete their section of the highway while other provinces still have not completed their sections? We think some statement should be made now as to what the policy and program is to be in that regard.
While I am not prepared to argue highway construction in connection with civil defence, I think we must recognize the fact that we in this country are spending large sums of money on civil defence. We all know,

of course, that highways and roads are one of the most important factors in connection with civil defence. Is the government going to assist the provinces to expand their highway systems on completion of their sections of the trans-Canada highway? I think that is one of the questions which must be answered soon by this government. We believe that a more realistic proposal than the one suggested in the amendment with which we are dealing here this evening would be one under which the federal government would assume 75 per cent of the total cost of the trans-Canada highway. That should include the cost of the right of way and the other costs in connection with the right of way such as the overpasses and the clover-leafs that are necessary on such a highway. The government should now make known its intention if it intends to provide an overall highway program in co-operation with the provinces, and that proposal should not be delayed. Canadians should know now whether or not the government is prepared to go forward with this integrated system of highways which we all expected would result from the legislation passed in this house in 1949.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
I should like to make a few brief remarks regarding this resolution, Mr. Chairman. I think it is appropriate that I should do so, as I come from a province which has exceptional difficulties in so far as the construction of main and arterial roads is concerned, and a province which historically has seen the development of settlements in that province based upon roads which have been constructed by senior governments. From the very earliest days of the history of the province of British Columbia, roads constructed by the military during the days of the gold rush into the Cariboo have been examples of what could be done by senior governments in the way of helping to develop and colonize a province.
It was due to the fact that a road had been constructed by the royal engineers at the time of the Cariboo gold rush that miners, after they had reached their destination and explored their claims, found that they could settle not only on the mainland but also on Vancouver island. It is very largely due to that initial effort in federal road construction that the development of British Columbia proceeded.
We have peculiar problems so far as British Columbia is concerned, because we are shut off from the rest of Canada by great mountain ranges which have only a limited number of passes, and it is because of that fact that one road leading from the prairies and eastern Canada is inadequate. One east-west road is not sufficient because of the
Trans-Canada Highway Act terrain and the fact that the various mountain ranges limit north-south communication. It is, therefore, of importance that there should be at least three main roads leading from eastern Canada into British Columbia.
Now, of course, we welcome the fact that some assistance is being given to the provincial government in the matter of road development. I do feel, like the previous speakers, that the assistance is rather meagre and it is coming rather late. I realize the great difficulties in the construction of the road. I believe that in British Columbia the trans-Canada highway is costing somewhere in the neighbourhood of $200,000 per mile, which of course is a very large sum of money. It is beyond the powers of even a province as prosperous as British Columbia to develop more than one road.
I refer also to the need for more than one road in relation to defence. We have to have the opportunity of moving, if necessary, by road not only in a direct line east and west, but also to the northeast into that great country north of Edmonton. All these roads have to be developed. One point which causes me some concern regarding the construction of the trans-Canada highway along its present route is the strength of the bridges on that route. The weight of military transport vehicles as well as that of civilian vehicles is increasing all the time. One hears of immense vehicles which have to be moved for military requirements that only the very strongest bridges could support. I feel that the type of bridge now being constructed, as I have seen them along the trans-Canada highway, would not carry the heaviest military vehicles. There is no other way to move these vehicles in many parts of our province except by road. I would therefore call that point to the attention of the parliamentary assistant.
One other point I should like to make concerns the ribbon development which is taking place on the outskirts of so many cities. I know that on the new portion of the trans-Canada highway out of Victoria there are innumerable auto courts, all kinds of stores and small buildings being constructed. If we are going to have that sort of ribbon development we will defeat one of the main objects of the trans-Canada highway as well as add to the risk of the loss of life on the highway, where school children and others will run across. I would hope it might be possible, in view of the money which is being spent by the federal government, for the federal government to reach some agreement with the provinces, and possibly with the municipalities as well, to prevent this very serious handicap which is now arising, namely the ribbon development

Trans-Canada Highway Act on the outskirts of cities along the new portions of the trans-Canada highway.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Humboldt-Melfort, Mr. Chairman, has presented this party's general position with regard to this resolution. He dealt with some of the criticisms of the resolution and made some suggestions. I support his remarks and the position he has taken. In order to save the time of the house I am not going to repeat them, but I do want to deal with the situation of the trans-Canada highway as it affects the residents of the southern interior of British Columbia.
In British Columbia we are anxious, as the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich said, that there should be three highways across the province, but in the meantime we are particularly concerned about getting our first trans-Canada section completed. Everyone knows that in British Columbia we are faced with unusual physical difficulties, first with regard to selecting the right route and second with respect to the cost of construction. I wish to deal with a particular aspect of this question because it is of extreme importance and concern to the residents of southeastern British Columbia. I have been asked by a number of organizations in that area to put forward their views at the first opportunity.
The problem that is of particular concern is the route that will be finally chosen between Revelstoke and Mount Eisenhower. We are also concerned because a great part of that route will no doubt be included in this 10 per cent of abnormal costs. To date there have been three possible routes suggested between those two points. The first is the Big Bend highway, which has been in operation as a dirt road since 1941, if I remember correctly. Now there is to be a reconsideration of that route, owing to the proposals for the building of the Mica creek and other dams on the Columbia. The other route that has been under consideration is the Rogers pass route paralleling the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway between Revelstoke and Golden.
The third route that has received some consideration and a great deal of publicity and support' in the interior of British Columbia is known as the Jumbo pass route, going from approximately Windermere in the upper Columbia valley across the divide of the Selkirks and the Purcells, which are a spur of the Selkirks, to the southern end of Howser lake and north along Trout lake and upper Arrow lake and then into Revelstoke. This route was surveyed at one time by engineers of the Canadian Pacific Railway when they were considering the main line of that railway, and it was given up because of the desire


of the company and of the government of the day, I understand, to choose the present route through the Kicking Horse pass. However, we have engineers in our district who are well acquainted with the area.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am coming to that point, and I am going to read some correspondence. We are unable to say who is going to make the choice, because I think the federal government has a finger in the pie at this stage of the investigation, and possibly the Canadian Pacific Railway. On account of the public interest in this question and the knowledge of the long-time engineers in the district, Mr. Boyd Affleck, a highly qualified engineer, and incidentally a very prominent supporter of the party to my left- he is a gentleman who is a strong opponent of the Kaiser dam-made an examination of the route from Howser lake to the Windermere area. As a result of that examination the provincial government undertook a reconnaissance survey a year or two ago between those two points. Since that time the associated boards of trade of British Columbia, together with other organizations and farmers' organizations, have been urging the provincial government to undertake a thorough survey of the route before any final decision is made with respect to the section of the trans-Canada highway that would connect Revelstoke with Mount Eisenhower on the trans-Canada. So far they have met with very little success.
* I raised the question in the house a few times, and the minister has always indicated that the choice of the route comes within the jurisdiction of the provincial government. All the federal government requires is that it be the shortest practicable route. Our organizations are very concerned about it, because we feel we have the time to thoroughly investigate all routes, that when you come to make a decision which will involve the expenditure of between $30 million and $50 million, when that decision will affect British Columbia seriously and all persons who use the route in years to come, every possible route shall be thoroughly investigated.
Now, to come back to the point the parliamentary assistant raised, I want to read two or three letters of recent date. The first was addressed by Mr. W. J. D. Walker, for the Kaslo board of trade, to Hon. Robert Winters,

Minister of Public Works, Ottawa, dated February 20, 1956. This is what he had to say:
Dear Sir:	re: Trans-Canada Highway
We notice that you have been quoted in the Revelstoke Review of February 2 as saying, "The Rogers pass is the answer and I have said so".
I read the same report. I continue with the letter:
This relates to the final choice of routes for the trans-Canada highway where it crosses the Selkirk range in British Columbia.
We do not have an additional copy of the above newspaper but we enclose a copy of the article in which you are quoted for your information.
You will note that they quote from an editorial in the Calgary Albertan which in turn quotes the Financial Times of Montreal which quotes your statement as above.
We would be glad if you would look into this and advise us if the statement attributed to you is correct or otherwise, and when and where it was made. It can happen that items taken from the context of a speech or article can be misconstrued. We have no wish at this time to be critical of the statement, or certainly not until we have first referred the matter direct to you.
As you are possibly aware we are a member of the associated boards of trade and chambers of commerce of southeastern British Columbia and as such are vitally interested in the ultimate and inevitable growth of the Kootenays. Through that body we, and all other member boards, have for several years now been advocating the thorough investigation of the Jumbo pass route as a possible alternative for the trans-Canada crossing of the Selkirks. Last fall the associated boards presented a brief to the British Columbia provincial cabinet demanding a survey of that route so that a full and proper comparison can be made of all alternative routes. When the taxpayers' dollar is to be spent to the tune of from $25 to $50 millions for such a project we feel that such a demand is fully justified, and we feel sure that when you consider it you will agree.
We would appreciate your early reply.
Yours truly,
W. J. D. Walker,
for Jumbo pass committee.
To that letter the minister replied on February 27, as follows:
Dear Mr. Walker:	re: Trans-Canada Highway
This will acknowledge receipt of your letter of February 20, on the above mentioned subject.
The situation is that under the terms of the agreement, the provincial governments determine the route of the trans-Canada highway, subject to our approval. In 1949, the governments of British Columbia and Alberta jointly decided that the route would go through Calgary to Banff, then by way of Kicking Horse pass to Revelstoke, and thence to Vancouver and Victoria by way of Nanaimo.
That route was accepted, and a considerable amount of work has been done on it. It involves, as you know, the Big Bend route between Golden and Revelstoke. The highway distance involved is some 190 miles, whereas the airline distance between Golden and Revelstoke is of the order of 90 miles.
It seemed to me from the start that it would be justifiable to spend some effort in trying to find a suitable pass between Golden and Revelstoke as an alternative to the Big Bend route. The Rogers pass seems to provide such an alternative.
Trans-Canada Highway Act
The situation, therefore, is not that an entirely new route is being sought in British Columbia, but simply that an effort is being made to have the highway conform to the definition laid down in the agreement that it should constitute the shortest practical east-west highway along the designated route, which, as I have told you, was specified by the provincial governments in 1949 and agreed to by the federal government.
Yours very truly,
Robert Winters.
It is a very odd thing, Mr. Chairman, from our point of view, that the minister says the provincial government has the final say. I want to tell him that every engineer of the federal department of works is preaching the Rogers pass route, and every Canadian Pacific official in the area has also been preaching the Rogers pass route, which will, of course, parallel the Canadian Pacific tracks between Revelstoke and Golden.
Before concluding, I just wish to read the reply to the minister's letter, dated March 10, 1956:
The Hon. Robert Winters,
Minister of Public Works,
Parliament Buildings,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
Re: Trans-Canada Highway
We acknowledge with thanks your letter of February 27th in reply to ours of February 20th.
From reading your letter our impression is that you favour use of the Rogers pass as an alternative to the present Big Bend route. However, you do not give any specific answer to our question concerning your statement that was quoted by the Financial Times of Montreal which was in turn quoted by the Calgary and Revelstoke papers and of which we furnished copies.
Also you made	no	mention of	your	reaction tothe possible use	of	the Jumbo	pass	as another
alternative route for the trans-Canada highway.
In the fourth	paragraph of	your	letter youmention that you felt it justifiable to spend some effort in trying	to	find a suitable	alternative
route to the Big Bend. As a result of that the Rogers pass was surveyed in 1955 and you now have complete technical data on two routes. It has been our firm contention all along that the third possible route, the Jumbo pass, should receive the same treatment the other two routes already have, namely a full survey so that proper comparisons can be made and to ensure that the final decision is a wise one.
When the route is chosen and constructed that will be a very final step, it will be too late then to rectify mistakes. As taxpayers it is our most emphatic opinion that when up to 50 million is to be spent for such a project all possible steps must be taken to see that it is spent wisely and for the benefit of the greatest number. Any other course would constitute a dire neglect of the duty of the government to the taxpayer.
You already have considerable data on the Jumbo pass submitted by the associated boards of trade of southeastern British Columbia and by certain member boards, and we will not elaborate further on it at this time other than to enclose a comparison chart of the three routes prepared by the Windermere district board of trade.

Trans-Canada Highway Act
We respectfully suggest that it would be your duty as the federal minister most concerned with this project to see that this matter is closely looked into and very carefully considered.
We shall await your reply with interest.
Yours very truly,
W. J. D. Walker,
for Jumbo pass committee
of the Kaslo board of trade.
This matter, Mr. Chairman, is of serious concern to the people of southeastern British Columbia. There is an unusual unanimous opinion that before any final decision is made the government of British Columbia and the federal government should undertake a thorough investigation of the Jumbo pass route.
I am not speaking tonight for one party or for one section. What I am saying tonight, Mr. Chairman, has the support of the residents of the southeastern portion of British Columbia, the various interested organizations and the great majority of hon. members of all political parties in that area. I think it is a fair request. They are not suggesting that this is the best route but the exploratory survey, the reconnaissance survey and the general knowledge of the topography possessed by qualified engineers, indicates it is a route that should be most carefully investigated before a final decision is made. That is all the people of southeastern British Columbia are asking.
I do urge that the parliamentary assistant and the minister give our representations very favourable consideration and do what we think is only prudent, wise and necessary; that is, undertake a thorough survey of the Jumbo pass route before a final decision is made as to the route of this section of the trans-Canada highway.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I certainly am not going to take very much of the committee's time tonight, but I would like to make a few remarks concerning this resolution.
In the first place, as has already been pointed out, there are some portions of the highway on which the route has not yet been decided. As far as I am concerned I would prefer to leave that decision to the engineers. I understand that both federal and provincial men are now working together in the investigation of the best possible route. I will certainly feel satisfied that with the provincial and federal governments working together they will come up with the best possible route for the trans-Canada highway.
I am not considering for a moment that the trans-Canada highway is the answer to our problem. I think, of course, that we should

have a trans-Canada highway system; however, that is not within the scope of the resolution.
I believe that British Columbia is going to spend $80 million this year in its highway program. A great deal of that money is going into the construction of east-west highways. We realize, of course, as has already been pointed out, that much money needs to be spent in British Columbia, particularly in those difficult sections of the country where we have to pass through the mountains and where a great deal of rock work is involved. I believe these things will be worked out in due course.
I still feel, and I think justifiably, that while the department is moving in the right direction in contributing 90 per cent of 10 per cent of the highway, its contribution remains inadequate. I believe we should have a trans-Canada highway financed by the federal government.
There is one other point which concerns me, and that is the co-operation between the Department of Public Works and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources as it has to do with the parks. I think we should now be budgeting for moneys to bring the park roads up to trans-Canada standards, not only those roads which pass through Banff and Yoho and the parks which trans-Canada will pass through but also in other parks such as Jasper. I think it is essential that there be co-operation between the two departments in having a through road for trucking and the free-wheeling of motor vehicles through these parks.
I cannot understand why trucks should be denied the right to travel on the roads in national parks through the mountains of British Columbia. They should not be told, "Trucks cannot go through here; this is only a tourist attraction". The passes through the mountains are in the vicinity of parks, particularly in the cases of Banff and Jasper. We must therefore have some co-operation and co-ordination between the departments in order to ensure that when trans-Canada is built and the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia have fulfilled their obligation, we are not going to have a bottleneck in the parks.
According to the report which I have in my hand dated March 31, 1955, it is evident that at the present time we are behind schedule in the building of the trans-Canada highway through the parks. I would urge that the government acquaint itself with the situation, knowing full well that once the green light is given to the government of British Columbia in respect of building their share of the highway, much pressure will be

brought to bear to get it finished. We would not like to see a situation where the Alberta and British Columbia sections were finished and we had a bottleneck for which the parks administration were responsible.

maintopic: WAYS AND MEANS
subtopic: TRANS-CANADA HIGHWAY ACT AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR HIGHER CONTRIBUTION TO COSTS OF HIGHWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in connection with this discussion of the resolution which stands in the name of the Minister of Public Works to provide for an increased federal contribution to the cost of construction of the trans-Canada highway, I think there are a number of things that have to be said. The first of these is a somewhat critical comment to the effect that there is no field in the general realm of national development in connection with which this government deserves more criticism than in the field of trans-Canada highway policy. The federal contribution is so insignificant as to amount to practically nothing. The lack of a trans-Canada highway is one of the most serious deficiencies in any program of national development, particularly in any program for the co-ordination of movement between provinces.
It is interesting to recall that the question of contributions by the dominion government to the cost of highways generally in Canada was first mooted in this house as long ago as 1912 under the government of Sir Robert Borden, when it was proposed that the dominion government should make contributions to the provinces on a per capita basis toward the cost of road construction. That bill passed the House of Commons but was defeated in the Senate. You will recall that in 1911 there had been a change of government after a long period under the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. The political complexion of the house changed but the political complexion of the Senate remained as it had been since 1896, and the other chamber saw fit to defeat the bill introduced by the government and passed by the house.
The government introduced the same bill in 1913 to provide for federal contributions to the cost of highway construction in the provinces, but that bill suffered exactly the same fate. It passed the House of Commons but was defeated in the Senate. Of course the outbreak of the first world war in 1914 shelved proposals of that nature. The record is that the first proposal for federal government contributions to the cost of highway construction was brought in by the government of Sir Robert Borden and put through the House of Commons.
It is significant to recall that since 1913 the Liberal government, of which the present government is a descendant, has been in power for 28 years, with a Conservative government for only five years, regrettably of course. Out of that we would take the period 67509-161
Trans-Canada Highway Act of the war. Taking into account or not including the period of the war and the immediate first post-war years, we find that since 1921 this government or its predecessors, those who follow the policies of the party of which hon. members opposite forming the government are members, have been in power for 28 of those years and we have not yet got a trans-Canada highway.
It is late enough for this government or any government to be bringing in this halfway measure which is preceded by the resolution now before the house, which reads:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act . . .
Expedient? It has been a necessity for many years, but the government is just getting around to introducing a half-hearted measure designed to make it possible to complete the trans-Canada highway. They still do not contemplate it being completed until 1961, because in the resolution it is stated that the cut-off date will be May 31, 1961. They still are not prepared to take all the measures necessary to ensure that the trans-Canada highway will be completed by 1961 because there is a term of the proposed legislation which does not appear on the face of the resolution. The resolution provides:
. . . that the Minister of Finance may pay a higher contribution for a portion of the highway in a province not exceeding 10 per centum thereof . . .
We know as a matter of fact that the bill to be based on the resolution will provide that the federal government may pay up to 90 per cent of the actual cost of construction in a province, but not for more than 10 per cent of the length of the highway in that province. So this government is not yet ready in this year 1956 to accept its responsibility of ensuring that there shall be an adequate system of coast to coast communication in Canada. It is still a pass the buck measure. Having grabbed all the tax resources, having grabbed the financial buck, they pass the political buck back to the provinces.
That is the attitude of this government, and that has been its attitude throughout toward this vital question of the responsibility for ensuring a coast to coast highway system in Canada. The program of this government falls short of what is necessary, and it is interesting to compare the situation in Canada with that in the United States where they have had a federal highway system and a federal highway program in being for some 50 years. That federal highway system and federal highway program have resulted in the development and construction, if my information is correct-this subject was sprung on us without notice, and it has not been possible to gather together all the information one

The Royal Assent
might have available in his files-of at least ten main east and west roads and some 30 or 40 main north and south roads, a total of some 40 federal highways in the United States of America.
We in Canada have not yet one trans-Canada highway, not one. This measure will not provide adequately for the completion of that one trans-Canada road by 1961. The inadequacy of the proposal of the dominion government to pay up to 90 per cent of the cost of a maximum of 10 per cent of the length of one highway in any province can readily be understood when you look at the situation in the province of British Columbia.
I believe that in Canada there are two provinces which face the maximum of difficulty and cost in connection with road construction, these being Ontario and British Columbia. British Columbia is faced with the highest per-mile cost of road construction of any province in Canada. Taking the east and west roads, there are four major mountain ranges to cross. Starting on the east are the Rocky mountains with peaks up to 12,000 feet. Then there is the Selkirk range with peaks up to 10,000 to 11,000 feet. Then comes the interior plateau, on which my own constituency is situated, made up of rough terrain, broken rocky hills with some level valleys but still offering a difficult problem in road construction. Then comes the Cascades range with peaks up to 8,000 to 9,000 feet and then the coast range which comes within .a few miles of the narrow coastal belt along the Pacific coast. So there are those four major mountain ranges to cross.

speechtext:
The house resumed consideration in committee of the following resolution-Mr. Winters-Mr. Applewhaite in the chair:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Trans-Canada Highway Act to provide that the Minister of Finance may pay a higher contribution for a portion of the highway in a province not exceeding ten per centum thereof; to extend contributions to costs incurred up to December 31, 1960 and to terminate all contributions on May 31, 1961; and to provide further that
the aggregate of all expenditures under the act may be increased to a maximum of two hundred and fifty million dollars.

speechtext:
1.	How are the concessions that include the sale o 1 handicrafts and souvenirs administered in the national parks of Canada?
2.	What are the dates, terms, names of contractees and length of said concessions, in Fundy national park, New Brunswick?
3.	What efforts are made to encourage the sale of local enterprise in said concessions?
Answer by: Mr. Lesage:
1.	Concessionaires who hold a lease or licence of occupation on public lands that have been made available for business purposes may obtain a licence to sell handicrafts and souvenirs under authority of the national parks business regulations.
2.	There is only one lease or licence on public land in Fundy park in connection with which a business licence for the sale of handicrafts and souvenirs has been taken out. This was a lease issued to Oliver William Robert Smith and Marie Annie Helen Smith for lot 3, block 1, Fundy park townsite, for a term of 42 years from October 1, 1954, to September 30, 1996, at an annual rental of $20 with provision for review of rental at ten-year intervals. The business licence to cover the sale of handicrafts and souvenirs is issued annually at a fee of $15.
3.	The choice of articles to be sold is considered to be the concern of the person operating the business. It is left entirely to the discretion of the concessionaire, provided that the terms of the business licence are observed.

1.	Has the Department of Fisheries made any survey of the Aluminum Company of Canada at Kitimat to determine any damage that might be done to the fishing industry by the operation of that development?
2.	If so, to what extent?
3.	Will the waste from the plant or town contaminate or pollute the waters to affect the fishing industry?
Answer by: Mr. Sinclair:
1.	Yes.
2.	Before the project was commenced engineers and biologists of the Department of Fisheries and of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission spent almost two years assessing possible damage to fisheries from the whole project which involved the Kitimat plant and in designing remedial measures. As construction proceeded, each step was checked including the water supply to the town, sewage and other discharge.
3.	Officials of the department are of opinion that the waste discharge will not affect fishing. This is being closely watched.
